isolate.narration: Filter ${var.field} for the value that stood out. In its Top values, click the + next to it. (Add filter works too.)

demonstration.narration: I'll filter ${var.field} to the value that stood out in its Top values.
demonstration.reasoning: The window mixes that traffic with healthy requests elsewhere. A filter pill keeps only that value, and its × removes it again.
demonstration.evidence: The ${var.field}: ${param.incident.finding} pill keeps only those records, and the hit count shows how many requests remain. Opening one will show whether they are the failing ones.

hints: Filter on the value that stood out in the Top values, not one you assumed.
Open ${var.field}'s Top values and click the + next to the value that stood out. That adds a filter pill for it. (Add filter, with the operator ‘is’, works too.)
Filter ${var.field} for ${param.incident.finding} with the + in its Top values; Show me can do it for you.

drifts.note: You filtered on ${action.field}: ${action.value}. Check whether that value is really where most of the failures are.

demonstration.narration: I'll open one failed request to check its endpoint or service and its error details together.
demonstration.reasoning: A total can look convincing even when it includes other records. Opening one typical event shows the key values together, which a count alone can't do.
demonstration.evidence: This one failed request has ${param.incident.finding}, status ${param.incident.status} and ${param.incident.error_type} together. So the filtered count isn't mixing in other failures. ${truth.conclusion}

goal.title: See where most requests go
goal.concept: A field's Top values count every request in the window. They show where most traffic goes, so you don't have to guess.
goal.narration: The report doesn't say which endpoint or service is failing. Open the ${var.field} field in the sidebar and read its Top values. Which value do most of the window's requests share?
goal.reasoning: Filtering on a guessed endpoint would assume the answer. The Top values show where most of the window's traffic really goes.
goal.evidence: The field's Top values show one value carrying far more of the window than any other.

demonstration.narration: The report doesn't say which endpoint or service is failing. I'll check ${var.field} Top values to see where most of this window's requests go.
demonstration.reasoning: Filtering on a guessed endpoint would assume the answer. Top values count every request in the window, so the next filter comes from the data.
demonstration.evidence: The highlighted row, ${param.incident.finding}, has most of the window's requests, well ahead of every other ${var.field} value. That is where to look for the errors since the release, so it's the value to filter on.

hints: Let the data show where the failing requests are, instead of assuming an endpoint.
Open the ${var.field} field in the sidebar and read its Top values (or add it as a column).

drifts.note: You opened ${action.field}. This step is about where most of the window's requests go.
You filtered before reading ${var.field}'s Top values, so the filter rests on a guess.

goal.title: Keep only the server errors
goal.concept: A range query matches every value between two limits. So one query catches every 5xx status code, whatever the exact code.
goal.narration: Busy isn't the same as failing. Keep only the server errors. In the query bar, use a range on http.response.status_code that takes every code from 500 up.
goal.reasoning: HTTP 5xx codes are server errors, and a release can produce any of them. A range catches them all, where a filter for one code would miss the rest.
goal.evidence: Only server errors remain, so what's left is this traffic's failures rather than all of it.

demonstration.narration: Busy isn't the same as failing. I'll keep only the server errors with a range query on the status code.
demonstration.reasoning: HTTP 5xx codes are server errors, and a release can produce any of them. http.response.status_code >= 500 catches every one, where a filter for a single code would miss the rest.
demonstration.evidence: Every request left is a server error. The hit count now counts this traffic's failures, not all of it, and the histogram shows when they began. Opening one will show which error they carry.

hints: Keep every server error, whatever its exact code, and nothing that succeeded.
KQL compares numbers with >, >=, < and <=. In the query bar, a range on http.response.status_code from 500 up keeps every 5xx code. (Add filter with ‘is between’ 500 and 599 works too.)
Type http.response.status_code >= 500; Show me can do it for you.
